chi_tiet.tieu_de: Every Type of Crab Explained in 9 Minutes
chi_tiet.mo_ta:
#Crabs #Wildlife #AnimalFacts

One of these is a hermit crab that outgrew every shell in the ocean, so it hardened its own body and stopped looking. One is blind, lives in permanent darkness, and grows its own food on its own arms. One holds a living sea anemone in each claw, and when researchers took one away, it tore the other in half and waited for both halves to grow back.

Eight crabs, eight completely different answers to the same problem.

This is every type of crab explained.

Two of the most repeated facts about these animals are wrong, and this video says so. The fiddler crab does not switch claws: the story that the small one grows into a new big claw on the opposite side was traced back through decades of citation in 2019 and found to rest on no evidence at all. What actually happens is stranger, and it is a bluff. And the last animal on the list is not a crab at all, and has not been one for 445 million years.

chi_tiet.tieu_de: Every Rare Animal Mutation Explained in 8 Minutes
chi_tiet.mo_ta:
#Mutations #Animals #AnimalFacts

A rat snake in Tennessee had two heads, and the two did not cooperate. They struck at prey separately, they swallowed separately, and one of them ate two to four times more than the other in a given meal, across two feeding seasons, with the same genome in both. Then the X-rays came back and made it stranger. That snake had two stomachs.

A cat is built for eighteen toes. The record holder has twenty-nine. And the mutation behind the famous ones is not inside a gene at all — it sits in a switch a million bases away from the gene it controls, and the whole thing is a single letter.

Look at the eye of an albino animal. It is not red. It is transparent, and the red you are looking at is the blood behind it.

This is every rare animal mutation explained.

And a lot of what gets written about these animals is a little bit wrong. This video says where.

There is no black panther species. The name covers two different cats on two continents carrying two unrelated mutations — dominant in the jaguar, recessive in the leopard. And the spots never went anywhere. A team in Malaysia rebuilt a camera trap to hold night mode in broad daylight, and the rosettes came back out of the dark.

The famous photograph of a yellow king penguin was never diagnosed. Four specialists were asked what the bird had and they did not agree: two said leucistic, one said albino, and the bird curator at the Natural History Museum in Tring said it is none of those. And the yellow was never the mutation anyway: a king penguin builds its yellow out of a pigment that appears to be chemically unique among birds, so taking the black away leaves it almost untouched.

The blue eye of a white cat does not cause its deafness. One dominant gene for white produces both, separately. The eye is a flag, not a cause.

And the zebra foal covered in dots that goes around every couple of years? No scientist ever published a word about that particular animal. What was published is better: seven genomes, and what they said was inbreeding.
